title: North Carolina Civics & Government (10th Grade)
description: North Carolina Civics & Government (10th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.question: The Declaration of Independence argues that governments are legitimate only when they rule with the:
questions.correctAnswer: Consent of the governed - the people are the source of all political authority
distractors: Permission of a hereditary monarch
Approval of the military's generals
Support of the wealthiest citizens
questions.explanation: Jefferson's argument, drawn from John Locke, is that government power comes from the people and exists to secure their rights. When a government destroys those rights instead, the people may alter or abolish it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Power flows UP from the people - consent is the foundation.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of citizens in 1776 dress gathered beneath a newly raised liberty pole on a town green, looking up with hope, a printed broadside kept unreadable in one man's hand. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Consent of the governed: the people are the source of government power.
img.title: POWER FROM THE PEOPLE

questions.question: Natural rights, as the founding generation understood them, are rights that:
questions.correctAnswer: People are born with and no government may justly take away - life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
distractors: Parliament grants to loyal subjects as a reward
Each state constitution creates for its own citizens only
Citizens earn by paying taxes for ten years
questions.explanation: The Declaration calls these rights 'unalienable' - they belong to people by nature, before any government exists. Government's job is to secure rights it did not create and therefore cannot rightfully destroy.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Natural rights are born with you - government protects them, it does not hand them out.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a newborn's hand resting beside an open palm and a rising sun breaking over a horizon, symbolic of rights that exist from birth, quiet and dignified. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Natural rights are inborn and unalienable - life, liberty, pursuit of happiness.
img.title: RIGHTS YOU ARE BORN WITH

questions.question: North Carolina's own Declaration of Rights opens its constitution with a distinctive phrase, declaring that all persons are endowed with rights including 'the enjoyment of the fruits of their own ____.'
questions.correctAnswer: Labor
distractors: Land
Learning
Loyalty
questions.explanation: Section 1 of the NC Declaration of Rights echoes the US Declaration but adds a phrase all its own: life, liberty, 'the enjoyment of the fruits of their own labor,' and the pursuit of happiness - a right later NC courts have cited in economic-liberty cases.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: NC added your paycheck to the list - fruits of your own labor.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a farmer, a blacksmith, and a teacher each holding the tools of their trade at sunrise in a Carolina town, dignity of work as the theme, mountains behind. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC's Declaration of Rights protects 'the enjoyment of the fruits of their own labor.'
img.title: FRUITS OF YOUR LABOR

questions.question: Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense (1776) changed American opinion mainly by:
questions.correctAnswer: Making a plain-language case that independence from Britain was both necessary and achievable
distractors: Publishing the first draft of the Constitution
Proving that France would win the war for America
Listing the grievances later copied into the Bill of Rights
questions.explanation: Paine wrote in direct language ordinary people could read, attacking monarchy itself and arguing a small island could not justly rule a continent. The pamphlet sold enormously and moved fence-sitters toward independence in 1776 - the same year North Carolina acted at Halifax.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Common Sense spoke plainly - and plain speech moved a continent.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a small printed pamphlet being read aloud by candlelight in a crowded colonial tavern, listeners leaning in, the cover kept blank and unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Common Sense made the plain-language case for independence.
img.title: COMMON SENSE

questions.question: The Magna Carta (1215) matters to American founding principles because it established the precedent that:
questions.correctAnswer: Even the king is subject to the law - government power can be limited in writing
distractors: Parliaments must meet every year
Colonies have the right to self-government
All men may vote for their rulers
questions.explanation: Forced on King John by his barons, the Magna Carta said the king could not imprison freemen or take property except by the law of the land. That idea - rulers bound by written law - traveled through English law into the founding documents of both the United States and North Carolina.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Magna Carta's big idea: the ruler is under the law, not above it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of medieval barons in 1215 presenting a large sealed charter to a reluctant king in a meadow camp beside a river, the charter's writing suggested but not readable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Magna Carta established that even kings are bound by the law.
img.title: THE KING UNDER LAW

questions.question: The Mayflower Compact (1620) is an early American example of:
questions.correctAnswer: A social contract - people creating a government by their own agreement to obey just laws
distractors: A royal charter granting land to a company
A military alliance with Native nations
A constitution written by a king's council
questions.explanation: Before landing, the Pilgrims signed an agreement to form a 'civil body politic' and enact just and equal laws for the general good. It is a founding-era root of self-government by consent, echoed later in state documents like North Carolina's.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No king told them to - the Pilgrims agreed on government themselves.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of men in 1620 dress signing a compact document aboard a dim wooden ship cabin, lanterns swaying, the writing on the page suggested but not readable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Mayflower Compact was self-government by agreement - a social contract.
img.title: GOVERNMENT BY AGREEMENT

questions.question: The English Bill of Rights (1689) influenced American founders by protecting, among other things:
questions.correctAnswer: Free elections, freedom of speech in Parliament, and a ban on cruel and unusual punishments
distractors: Universal voting rights for all adults
The right of colonies to print their own money
Freedom of religion for every English subject
questions.explanation: After the Glorious Revolution, Parliament required William and Mary to accept limits: no standing army without consent, free elections, speech protected in Parliament, and no cruel and unusual punishments. Several of these phrases reappear nearly word-for-word in the US Bill of Rights and state declarations of rights.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1689 England wrote limits the founders borrowed - including 'cruel and unusual.'

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a 1689 parliamentary chamber with members presenting a formal declaration scroll to a king and queen seated on thrones, candles and dark wood paneling, writing suggested but not readable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The English Bill of Rights modeled limits later copied into American rights documents.
img.title: BORROWED LIMITS

questions.question: The Articles of Confederation failed as a national government chiefly because the Confederation Congress could not:
questions.correctAnswer: Tax, regulate trade between the states, or enforce its decisions on the states
distractors: Hold elections for its own members
Declare war or make treaties
Admit new states to the Union
questions.explanation: Congress under the Articles could ask states for money but not compel payment, could not regulate interstate commerce, and had no executive or national courts to enforce its acts. Shays's Rebellion exposed the weakness and pushed leaders toward the Constitutional Convention.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A government that can only ask nicely is not much of a government.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of thirteen separate candles on a table, each burning alone with gaps between them, one nearly out, in a dark meeting room - symbolism of disunity. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Articles gave Congress no power to tax, regulate trade, or enforce decisions.
img.title: TOO WEAK TO GOVERN

questions.question: Under the Articles of Confederation, amending the Articles required:
questions.correctAnswer: Unanimous agreement of all thirteen states - one reason needed changes proved impossible
distractors: A two-thirds vote of Congress alone
Approval by the president of Congress
A majority vote of the people in a referendum
questions.explanation: Article XIII required every state legislature to confirm any amendment. Even a widely supported impost (tariff) failed when a single state objected. The founders replaced this rigidity with Article V of the Constitution: two-thirds to propose, three-fourths to ratify.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Thirteen yeses or nothing - unanimity froze the Articles in place.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a long council table with thirteen chairs, twelve pushed in and one chair tipped backward empty, symbolizing a single holdout blocking agreement. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Amending the Articles needed all 13 states - unanimity blocked reform.
img.title: ONE HOLDOUT BLOCKS ALL

questions.question: James Madison's Federalist No. 10 argues that the best way to control the dangers of factions is:
questions.correctAnswer: A large republic, where many competing interests make it hard for any one faction to dominate
distractors: Banning political parties by law
Letting only property owners vote
Keeping the country small and uniform
questions.explanation: Madison defined a faction as a group driven by passion or interest against the rights of others. Since factions cannot be eliminated without destroying liberty, he argued their effects must be controlled - and an extended republic with many interests does exactly that.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Madison's cure for factions: make the republic bigger, not the people quieter.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a vast landscape with many different towns, farms, ports, and workshops under one sky, connected by roads, symbolizing one large diverse republic. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federalist No. 10: a large republic controls factions by multiplying interests.
img.title: THE LARGE REPUBLIC

questions.question: Federalist No. 51 explains the separation of powers with the famous idea that:
questions.correctAnswer: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition' - each branch is given the tools and motives to resist the others
distractors: Judges should referee all disputes between branches
The president must approve every act of Congress twice
States will naturally keep the federal government honest
questions.explanation: Madison argued the Constitution does not rely on officials being angels: 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.' Each branch defends its own power, and that rivalry - built into the structure - protects liberty.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No angels available - so the branches watch each other.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three balanced stone pillars leaning against one another in a stable triangular structure, each holding the others up, classical architecture style. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federalist No. 51: ambition counteracts ambition through checks and balances.
img.title: AMBITION VS. AMBITION

questions.question: Anti-Federalists opposed ratifying the Constitution in 1787-88 mainly because they feared:
questions.correctAnswer: A powerful central government without a bill of rights would crush liberty and state authority
distractors: The Constitution gave too much power to the states
Elections would be held too frequently
The new government would abolish the presidency
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists warned that a distant national government with taxing and military power, and no enumerated protections for rights, invited tyranny. Their pressure produced the promise - and then the reality - of the Bill of Rights in 1791.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Anti-Federalists demanded a bill of rights - and history proved them useful.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of farmers and craftsmen debating heatedly in a 1788 town meeting house, one standing with a raised hand of warning, winter light through the windows. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Anti-Federalists feared a strong central government without a bill of rights.
img.title: THE SKEPTICS' WARNING

questions.question: North Carolina's Hillsborough Convention of 1788 took a position almost unique in the ratification struggle: the delegates:
questions.correctAnswer: Refused to ratify OR reject, demanding a declaration of rights and amendments first
distractors: Ratified the Constitution faster than any other state
Voted to join South Carolina instead
Burned their copies of the Constitution in protest
questions.explanation: By a wide margin, Hillsborough voted neither to ratify nor reject but to insist on a declaration of rights and 20-plus proposed amendments. The strategy worked: Congress proposed the Bill of Rights in 1789, and North Carolina then ratified at Fayetteville that November. The FPCL course pairs this NC story with the national founding documents.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: NC held out for rights in writing - and got the Bill of Rights.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of delegates in 1788 standing firm with arms folded in a plain meeting hall, a document held closed in one leader's hand, determined expressions, summer heat haze outside. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Hillsborough neither ratified nor rejected - it demanded a declaration of rights first.
img.title: HOLDING OUT FOR RIGHTS

questions.question: The principle of limited government, shared by the US and North Carolina constitutions, means:
questions.correctAnswer: Government may exercise only the powers granted to it, and written constitutions mark the boundaries
distractors: Government should meet only part of the year
Only small towns may have governments
Officials may serve only one term in office
questions.explanation: A constitution is a grant of power with edges. Powers not granted are withheld - at the federal level by enumeration and the Tenth Amendment, and in North Carolina by a constitution that structures and confines every branch.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A constitution is a fence as much as a foundation.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a strong stone fence running along the edge of an open field of government buildings, the fence clearly marking a boundary, morning light. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Limited government: only granted powers, bounded by the written constitution.
img.title: POWER WITH EDGES

questions.question: A state official caught taking bribes argues that her high office should shield her from prosecution. The constitutional principle that answers her claim is the rule of law, because:
questions.correctAnswer: Laws apply equally to everyone, including the officials who enforce them
distractors: Only legislatures may prosecute crimes under separation of powers
Voters alone can punish officials, through elections
Federalism leaves state officials answerable to no court
questions.explanation: Rule of law means no one is above the law and no one is beneath its protection: laws are public, stable, and applied impartially. The NC Declaration of Rights expresses it in Section 35's call for 'a frequent recurrence to fundamental principles.'
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rule of law means the referee follows the rulebook too.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a balanced scale standing level on a courthouse steps with a sheriff and a farmer equally lit on either side, symbolizing impartial application of law. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Rule of law: laws apply equally, even to those who enforce them.
img.title: NO ONE ABOVE THE LAW

questions.question: Section 2 of the North Carolina Declaration of Rights declares that 'all political power is vested in and derived from the people.' This is the principle of:
questions.correctAnswer: Popular sovereignty
distractors: Divine right
Judicial supremacy
Nullification
questions.explanation: North Carolina's constitution states the American founding premise in so many words: the people hold the power and lend it to government. The same principle opens the US Constitution - 'We the People' - and underlies elections, amendments, and the right to reform government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: NC wrote it plainly - all political power comes from the people.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a great bell being raised by many hands of ordinary citizens together on ropes, a town square and church steeples behind, symbolism of collective power. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Popular sovereignty: all political power is derived from the people.
img.title: WE THE PEOPLE, NC STYLE

questions.question: Due process of law protects individuals by requiring that before government can punish or take property, it must:
questions.correctAnswer: Follow fair procedures - notice, a hearing, and an impartial decision-maker
distractors: Win a unanimous vote of the legislature
Pay the individual a fee for the inconvenience
Publish the accusation in a newspaper first
questions.explanation: Due process is the promise of fair process: the government must tell you the charge, let you be heard, and prove its case under known rules. The Fifth Amendment binds the federal government; the Fourteenth binds the states, and NC's 'law of the land' clause does the same work in state law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No shortcuts - fair notice, fair hearing, fair decision.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an open courtroom door with light streaming in, a notice pinned beside it kept blurred and unreadable, a gavel resting beside an open law book with blank pages. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Due process requires fair procedures before government may punish.
img.title: FAIR PROCESS FIRST

questions.question: North Carolina's Declaration of Rights uses the historic phrase 'the law of the land' in Section 19 to guarantee:
questions.correctAnswer: That no one may be deprived of rights except by lawful judgment - NC's own due process and equal protection guarantee
distractors: That landowners alone may hold public office
That all farmland is exempt from taxation
That state law can never be changed once written
questions.explanation: Section 19's 'law of the land' clause descends from the Magna Carta's language and has been read by NC courts as the state counterpart to due process and equal protection. FPCL students compare it directly with the Fourteenth Amendment - two documents, the same shield.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 'Law of the land' is NC's own due process clause - older than the Bill of Rights.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an ancient parchment scroll beside a modern constitution book on a judge's desk, a magnifying glass over a single paragraph kept unreadable, continuity across centuries as the theme. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Section 19's 'law of the land' clause is NC's due process and equal protection guarantee.
img.title: LAW OF THE LAND

questions.question: The Preamble to the US Constitution begins 'We the People of the United States, in Order to form a more perfect Union.' The phrase 'more perfect Union' signals that the Constitution was intended to:
questions.correctAnswer: Improve on the union created by the Articles of Confederation, not start from nothing
distractors: Unite the states into a single province under one governor
Perfect the alliance with Great Britain
End all differences among the states forever
questions.explanation: The framers saw themselves repairing a union that already existed but worked badly. The Preamble also lists the purposes - justice, tranquility, defense, welfare, liberty - that courts and citizens still cite to explain the Constitution's aims.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 'More perfect' - the framers were fixing a union, not founding from zero.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of craftsmen repairing and strengthening a great wooden bridge over a wide river while traffic continues to cross, scaffolding and new beams being fitted. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Preamble frames the Constitution as improving the Articles' union.
img.title: A MORE PERFECT UNION

questions.question: The Virginia Plan and the New Jersey Plan deadlocked the Constitutional Convention until the Connecticut Compromise settled the question of representation by creating:
questions.correctAnswer: A bicameral Congress - population-based House and equal-representation Senate
distractors: A single-house legislature elected by state governments
A Congress chosen entirely by the president
Representation based on each state's tax payments
questions.explanation: Large states wanted representation by population; small states wanted equality. The Great Compromise split the difference: the House apportioned by population, the Senate with two per state. North Carolina's own legislature mirrors the pattern in miniature - a population-based House (120) and Senate (50) elected from districts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Big states got the House, small states got the Senate - compromise built Congress.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a scale balancing two very different sized stone blocks level with each other through a clever beam arrangement, delegates' empty chairs behind. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Connecticut Compromise created a two-house Congress balancing population and equality.
img.title: THE GREAT COMPROMISE

questions.question: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted three-fifths of the enslaved population for representation and taxation. Today it is understood as:
questions.correctAnswer: A morally indefensible bargain that boosted slave-state power and was erased by the Fourteenth Amendment
distractors: A step toward emancipation supported by abolitionists
A rule still used in modern census counts
A compromise about trade duties on imports
questions.explanation: The compromise inflated the South's seats in the House and Electoral College for decades while treating enslaved people as fractions for others' power. Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment replaced it by counting 'the whole number of persons.' FPCL treats it as a founding flaw later corrected by amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A founding bargain built on injustice - corrected only by civil war and amendment.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an old ledger page with rows of tally marks crossed out and rewritten, a quill resting beside it, somber archival mood. Tallies shown as abstract marks without digits. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Three-Fifths Compromise inflated slave-state power; the 14th Amendment erased it.
img.title: A FOUNDING FLAW

questions.question: North Carolina's 1776 constitution, written at Halifax, differed sharply from the modern one. Its legislature was so dominant that it:
questions.correctAnswer: Elected the governor itself, for a one-year term, leaving the governor with little independent power
distractors: Gave the governor a lifetime appointment
Allowed the governor to dissolve it at will
Met only once every ten years
questions.explanation: Fresh from royal governors, the 1776 framers made the General Assembly supreme: it chose the governor annually and controlled most appointments. Experience taught balance - the 1835 reforms added popular election of the governor, and the veto did not arrive until 1996.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In 1776 NC trusted the legislature with nearly everything - even picking the governor yearly.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a colonial assembly hall with rows of legislators' desks arranged in a semicircle towering over one small single chair at the side, showing an imbalance of power. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Under the 1776 NC constitution, the legislature elected a weak governor yearly.
img.title: WHEN THE ASSEMBLY RULED

questions.question: A republic differs from a direct democracy in that in a republic:
questions.correctAnswer: Citizens elect representatives who make laws on their behalf
distractors: A king rules with the advice of elected nobles
All citizens vote on every law themselves
Laws are made by judges rather than legislators
questions.explanation: The United States and North Carolina are republics (representative democracies): the people hold sovereignty but exercise daily lawmaking through elected representatives, reserving direct votes for elections and constitutional referendums.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Republic = the people rule through representatives they elect.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of citizens in a town square shaking hands with their elected representative who carries their petitions toward a distant capitol, petitions kept blank and unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: In a republic, citizens govern through elected representatives.
img.title: RULE BY REPRESENTATIVES

questions.question: Section 35 of the NC Declaration of Rights says 'a frequent recurrence to fundamental principles is absolutely necessary to preserve the blessings of liberty.' In plain language, it instructs citizens to:
questions.correctAnswer: Regularly return to first principles and measure their government against them
distractors: Re-elect the same officials as often as possible
Hold constitutional conventions every year
Memorize the state constitution in school
questions.explanation: The clause is a standing instruction to each generation: reread the founding principles, compare the government's actual conduct, and correct course. It is the philosophical seed of the entire FPCL course - North Carolina students study founding documents so they can perform exactly this recurrence.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: NC's constitution tells every generation: go back to the principles and check.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a lighthouse beam sweeping back across dark water toward a rocky shore, symbolizing a recurring return to a fixed guiding point, night sky. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Section 35 calls for frequent return to fundamental principles to preserve liberty.
img.title: RETURN TO PRINCIPLES

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches a founding document to the principle it most clearly contributed?
questions.correctAnswer: English Petition of Right and Magna Carta tradition - limits on taxation and punishment without legal process
distractors: Mayflower Compact - the invention of judicial review
Articles of Confederation - a strong national executive
Common Sense - the structure of the federal court system
questions.explanation: The English inheritance - Magna Carta (1215) and the Petition of Right (1628) - taught that kings could not tax or imprison at whim. American founders layered colonial self-government (Mayflower Compact) and revolutionary argument (Common Sense) onto that foundation of limited, lawful government.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Layer by layer - English limits, colonial compacts, revolutionary arguments.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of stacked stone layers forming a foundation wall, each layer a different age and color of stone, a modern building rising from the top layer. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: English rights documents contributed limits on arbitrary taxation and punishment.
img.title: LAYERS OF LIBERTY

questions.question: Article I of the US Constitution establishes the legislative branch. Which power listed there belongs to Congress alone?
questions.correctAnswer: Declaring war
distractors: Commanding the armed forces in battle
Granting pardons for federal crimes
Appointing Supreme Court justices
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the powers to declare war, coin money, regulate interstate and foreign commerce, and raise armies. The president commands the forces Congress raises and funds - a deliberate separation of the sword from the purse.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress declares and funds; the president commands. Sword and purse in different hands.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of the United States Capitol building at dawn with its dome lit, an empty chamber of desks visible through tall glass in the foreground. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Congress alone holds the power to declare war.
img.title: THE POWER TO DECLARE WAR

questions.question: To become a United States senator, the Constitution requires a person to be at least 30 years old, a citizen for nine years, and:
questions.correctAnswer: An inhabitant of the state from which they are elected
distractors: A resident of the same congressional district for five years
A former member of the state legislature
The owner of property in the state capital
questions.explanation: Article I, Section 3 sets the Senate's qualifications: age 30, nine years a citizen, and inhabitancy in the state when elected. North Carolina's two senators represent the whole state, while its 14 House members represent districts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Senator = 30 years old, 9 years a citizen, living in the state.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a senate chamber with one hundred empty desks arranged in a semicircle, flags with blurred unreadable designs, marble columns. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Senators must be 30, citizens for 9 years, and inhabitants of their state.
img.title: WHO CAN BE A SENATOR

questions.question: A bill has passed both houses of Congress but the president vetoes it. Congress can still enact the bill by:
questions.correctAnswer: Overriding the veto with a two-thirds vote in each house
distractors: Sending it to the Supreme Court for approval
Holding a national referendum on the bill
Re-passing it with a simple majority after 30 days
questions.explanation: The veto override is a central check: two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate can make a bill law despite the president. Compare North Carolina, where the General Assembly overrides a governor's veto by three-fifths of each house - a lower bar that makes NC overrides more common.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal override needs two-thirds; North Carolina needs only three-fifths.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a large ceremonial pen lying crossed out on a desk while many hands raise in a vote behind it, legislative chamber blurred in the background. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Congress overrides a veto by two-thirds of each house; NC requires three-fifths.
img.title: OVERRIDING THE VETO

questions.question: The president's power to grant pardons for federal offenses is checked mainly by the fact that it:
questions.correctAnswer: Cannot be used in cases of impeachment - and cannot pardon state crimes at all
distractors: Requires Senate approval of two-thirds
Expires at the end of each calendar year
Must be reviewed by the Supreme Court within 90 days
questions.explanation: Article II's pardon power is broad but bounded: it reaches only federal offenses and expressly excludes impeachment cases. North Carolina's governor holds a parallel state pardon power for NC crimes - separate systems, separate sovereigns, a working picture of federalism.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two pardon powers, two sovereigns - president for federal crimes, governor for state crimes.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a prison gate opening at dawn with light beyond it, a sealed official document with a ribbon resting on a desk in the foreground, seal unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The presidential pardon reaches federal offenses only, never impeachment.
img.title: THE PARDON POWER

questions.question: Federal judges are appointed by the president with Senate confirmation and serve:
questions.correctAnswer: During good behavior - effectively for life, removable only by impeachment
distractors: Fixed eight-year terms like NC Supreme Court justices
Four-year terms renewable by the president
Until the next presidential election
questions.explanation: Life tenure insulates federal judges from political pressure, letting them rule against powerful officials without fearing for their jobs. North Carolina made the opposite choice: its Supreme Court justices, Court of Appeals judges, and Superior Court judges are elected by the voters to eight-year terms, and its District Court judges to four-year terms - independence versus accountability, weighed differently.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Federal judges serve for life; NC judges answer to voters - eight-year terms for appellate and superior court judges, four for district court.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two benches side by side, one of dark marble under a steady beam of light and one of warm wood beneath a window with voters' silhouettes outside, symbolic contrast. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federal judges serve for life; NC judges are elected - 8-year terms for appellate and superior courts, 4 for district court.
img.title: TWO WAYS TO CHOOSE JUDGES

questions.question: The Tenth Amendment reserves to the states or the people all powers that the Constitution neither delegates to the federal government nor prohibits to the states. This principle is called:
questions.correctAnswer: Reserved powers - the constitutional basis of state authority over schools, licensing, and elections
distractors: Enumerated powers
Implied powers
Concurrent powers
questions.explanation: Reserved powers are why North Carolina - not Washington - runs public schools, issues driver's licenses, and conducts elections. The FPCL course treats the Tenth Amendment as the hinge between the US Constitution and the NC Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: If the Constitution does not hand it to Washington, it stays with the states.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a large stone wall with a gate labeled by shape only, fields and a schoolhouse on the near side and a distant capital dome on the far side, morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to the states or the people.
img.title: RESERVED TO THE STATES

questions.question: Taxing citizens, building roads, and establishing courts are powers exercised by BOTH the federal and state governments. Such powers are called:
questions.correctAnswer: Concurrent powers
distractors: Exclusive powers
Denied powers
Implied powers
questions.explanation: Concurrent powers are shared: both levels tax, spend, borrow, build infrastructure, and run court systems. North Carolinians pay federal and state income taxes and can be tried in either system - federalism in everyday dress.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Concurrent = shared - both governments tax, build, and judge.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two overlapping circles of light projected on a wall, the bright overlap in the middle containing images of a road, a courthouse, and a tax form kept blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Concurrent powers are shared by federal and state governments.
img.title: SHARED POWERS

questions.question: The 'necessary and proper' clause of Article I, Section 8 is often called the elastic clause because it:
questions.correctAnswer: Stretches Congress's power to make all laws needed to carry out its enumerated powers
distractors: Allows Congress to amend the Constitution by statute
Permits states to stretch federal laws to fit local needs
Lets the president expand executive power in emergencies
questions.explanation: The clause grants implied powers: if the end is legitimate (say, regulating commerce), Congress may choose workable means (say, chartering a bank, as in McCulloch v. Maryland). It stretches - but it is anchored to the enumerated powers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Elastic, but tied down - implied powers must connect to listed powers.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a strong elastic band stretched between two fixed brass anchors labeled by position rather than words, holding a bundle of tools suspended in the middle. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The elastic clause grants implied powers tied to enumerated ends.
img.title: THE ELASTIC CLAUSE

questions.question: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), the Supreme Court struck down Maryland's tax on the national bank, holding that:
questions.correctAnswer: 'The power to tax involves the power to destroy' - states may not tax federal operations
distractors: States may tax any business operating within their borders
The national bank itself was unconstitutional
Congress had exceeded its power by creating a bank
questions.explanation: Chief Justice Marshall upheld the bank under the necessary and proper clause and barred state taxation of it under the supremacy clause. The case remains the classic statement that the Constitution created a government of the people, supreme within its sphere.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: States cannot tax the federal government out of existence - McCulloch settled it.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an imposing 1819 bank building of stone with a state tax collector's hand stopped mid-air at its gate, courthouse pillars rising behind, dramatic light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: McCulloch: states may not tax federal operations; the power to tax is the power to destroy.
img.title: THE POWER TO DESTROY

questions.question: The supremacy clause of Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties 'the supreme Law of the Land.' Its practical effect is that:
questions.correctAnswer: When a valid federal law conflicts with a state law, the federal law prevails
distractors: State constitutions override federal statutes
Federal judges must follow state court precedents
States may ignore federal laws they find unjust
questions.explanation: Supremacy resolves collisions: within the federal government's constitutional sphere, its law wins. A North Carolina statute that conflicts with a valid federal law cannot be enforced - state judges themselves are bound by Article VI to uphold federal law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Collisions happen - the supremacy clause is the traffic rule.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two stacks of law books, the taller stack casting its shadow over the shorter one on a judge's bench, a beam of light from above settling the order. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Valid federal law prevails over conflicting state law.
img.title: SUPREME LAW OF THE LAND

questions.question: North Carolina's constitution organizes its government in a familiar pattern: Article II covers the legislative branch, Article III the executive, and Article IV the:
questions.correctAnswer: Judicial branch - one constitution echoing the structure of the other
distractors: Finance and taxation
Local governments
Militia and military affairs
questions.explanation: North Carolina's constitution lays out legislature, executive, and judiciary in Articles II, III, and IV - one article later than the US Constitution's Articles I, II, and III, because North Carolina's Article I is its Declaration of Rights. FPCL standards (CL.C&G.2) ask students to analyze the branches at both levels side by side - the parallel structure is the lesson.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Same skeleton, two constitutions - the US uses Articles I, II, III; NC uses II, III, IV because its Article I is the Declaration of Rights.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two framed architectural blueprints side by side showing the same three-part floor plan drawn at different scales, one larger and one smaller, on a drafting table. Blueprints shown abstractly with no readable annotations. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC's Articles II, III, IV mirror the US structure: legislative, executive, judicial.
img.title: PARALLEL BLUEPRINTS

questions.question: Unlike the president, North Carolina's governor shares executive power with nine other separately elected officials. The strongest consequence of this plural executive is:
questions.correctAnswer: The governor cannot fire or control officials like the attorney general or treasurer - each answers to the voters directly
distractors: The governor has no power at all in North Carolina
State agencies may ignore all executive orders automatically
The Council of State can veto legislation by majority vote
questions.explanation: In NC, the attorney general, treasurer, auditor, and others hold independent electoral mandates. A governor who disagrees with the attorney general cannot remove them - accountability runs to the ballot box, not the governor's office. This is one of the sharpest structural contrasts in the FPCL course.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten bosses, all elected - the NC governor must persuade, not command.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a round table with ten equal chairs and ten separate doors leading into the room from different directions, symbolizing independent mandates. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC's plural executive: ten elected officials the governor cannot fire.
img.title: TEN INDEPENDENT OFFICIALS

questions.question: In most states the lieutenant governor is elected on a ticket with the governor. North Carolina instead elects its lieutenant governor:
questions.correctAnswer: Separately - so the governor and lieutenant governor can be, and have been, from different parties
distractors: By the General Assembly from among its own members
By appointment of the governor after inauguration
In a special election two years after the governor's race
questions.explanation: Separate election means North Carolina can - and repeatedly has - seated a governor of one party and a lieutenant governor of another. The lieutenant governor's constitutional roles include presiding over the state Senate and succeeding the governor if the office falls vacant.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Separate ballots can mean split parties at the top of NC government.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two separate ballot boxes side by side at a polling place, voters dropping one ballot in each, a divider between the two lines of voters. Ballots kept blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC elects its lieutenant governor separately from the governor.
img.title: SEPARATE BALLOTS, SPLIT TOP

questions.question: A governor serves a four-year term in North Carolina and may be re-elected. The state constitution limits the governor to:
questions.correctAnswer: Two consecutive elected terms - after a break, the person may run again
distractors: One term in a lifetime
Three consecutive terms
Unlimited consecutive terms like a legislator
questions.explanation: Article III limits a governor to succeeding themselves once consecutively (two four-year terms back to back), though nothing bars a later return after another governor serves. Legislators, by contrast, face no term limits at all in North Carolina.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two in a row, then sit one out - the NC governor's limit.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an hourglass with sand for exactly two full turns resting beside a row of identical chairs receding into the distance without limit, symbolic contrast. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC governors may serve two consecutive terms; legislators have no term limits.
img.title: TWO TERMS IN A ROW

questions.question: The impeachment process in the US Constitution gives the House of Representatives the power to impeach (bring charges) and the Senate the power to:
questions.correctAnswer: Conduct the trial, convicting only by a two-thirds vote
distractors: Issue the formal pardon after conviction
Appeal the case to the Supreme Court
Remove the official by majority vote without a trial
questions.explanation: Impeachment splits accusation from judgment: the House impeaches by majority; the Senate tries, with the Chief Justice presiding over presidential trials; conviction and removal require two-thirds. No president has ever been removed by this process.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House accuses, Senate judges - and two-thirds must agree to remove.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a formal trial chamber arranged with prosecutors' tables facing a long raised bench, an oath Bible on a cushion, solemn marble interior. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The House impeaches; the Senate convicts by two-thirds.
img.title: ACCUSE AND JUDGE

questions.question: The Electoral College gives North Carolina 16 electoral votes. That number equals:
questions.correctAnswer: Its total representation in Congress - 14 House seats plus 2 Senate seats
distractors: Its number of counties divided by six
The number of its state supreme court justices
Twice its number of Council of State members
questions.explanation: Each state's electors equal its congressional delegation. North Carolina gained a 14th House seat after the 2020 census, so it casts 16 electoral votes; a candidate needs 270 of 538 to win the presidency. State growth literally increases NC's voice in choosing presidents.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 14 plus 2 equals 16 - NC's weight in the Electoral College.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a large wall map of a state with fourteen district shapes in varied colors plus two gold stars above it, map kept abstract without labels, pins on a cork board. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC's 16 electoral votes = 14 House seats + 2 senators.
img.title: SIXTEEN ELECTORAL VOTES

questions.question: After each census, congressional and state legislative districts are redrawn. In North Carolina, drawing the maps is the constitutional job of:
questions.correctAnswer: The General Assembly, whose plans the governor cannot veto
distractors: The state Supreme Court, by a panel of retired judges
The governor, acting through an appointed commission
A citizens' commission chosen by lottery
questions.explanation: North Carolina assigns redistricting to the legislature itself, and unusually, redistricting bills are exempt from the governor's veto. That design has made NC map-drawing a recurring courtroom battleground over gerrymandering for four decades - state and federal courts have both intervened.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In NC the legislature draws its own maps - and the governor cannot veto them.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of hands drawing district boundary lines with a ruler and pencil across a large state map on a table, the lines forming odd shapes, map without labels or place names. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The General Assembly draws NC's districts; the governor cannot veto the maps.
img.title: WHO DRAWS THE MAPS

questions.question: Treaties made by the president take effect only after:
questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of the senators present concur (advise and consent)
distractors: A majority of the House of Representatives approves
All fifty governors sign the treaty
The Supreme Court certifies the treaty's fairness
questions.explanation: Article II divides foreign affairs: the president negotiates, but a supermajority of the Senate must consent before a treaty binds the nation. Executive agreements, by contrast, rest on the president's own authority and are far more common in modern practice.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The president proposes treaties; two-thirds of the Senate disposes.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two diplomats shaking hands across a polished table with a large unsigned document and two pens resting beside it, flags blurred in the background. Document kept unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Treaties require two-thirds Senate consent.
img.title: ADVISE AND CONSENT

questions.question: An executive order differs from a law because an executive order:
questions.correctAnswer: Is issued by the executive alone to manage the government, and can be reversed by a later executive or struck down if it exceeds legal authority
distractors: Requires a two-thirds vote of Congress to take effect
Can never be challenged in any court
Amends the Constitution directly
questions.explanation: Orders direct agencies within existing law and the Constitution - they are not statutes. Presidents and governors (including North Carolina's, in emergencies like hurricanes) use them for speed, but courts may void orders that outrun the law, and successors may revoke them with a signature.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fast but fragile - an order lives only within the law and the next executive's patience.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a single signature being written on an order form by a fountain pen, the form's text blurred and unreadable, an eraser resting pointedly beside the page. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Executive orders manage government within the law and can be reversed or struck down.
img.title: FAST BUT FRAGILE

questions.question: Judicial review - the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional - was established for the federal courts in:
questions.correctAnswer: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
distractors: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
questions.explanation: Deciding a dispute over last-minute judicial commissions, Chief Justice Marshall claimed for the courts the duty to say what the law is - and to void acts of Congress that conflict with the Constitution. North Carolina's courts exercise the same power over state law under the NC Constitution.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Marbury gave courts the red pen over unconstitutional laws.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a chief justice in 1803 dress writing an opinion at a wooden desk by oil lamp, a small stack of commission papers tied with ribbon beside the inkwell. Writing suggested, not readable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review.
img.title: THE RED PEN OF THE COURTS

questions.question: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) strengthened federal power by interpreting the commerce clause to cover:
questions.correctAnswer: Navigation and commercial intercourse among the states, not merely the buying and selling of goods
distractors: Only trade conducted on the high seas
Trade within a single state when prices seemed unfair
The manufacture of goods before they enter trade
questions.explanation: Marshall read 'commerce' broadly as intercourse and 'among the several states' as reaching inside state lines wherever interstate activity is concerned. The decision undercut state monopolies and laid the foundation for two centuries of federal regulatory power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Commerce means intercourse - Gibbons stretched federal power across state lines.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two rival steamboats racing on a wide river between two states' shores in 1824, smoke trailing, passengers crowding the rails, a broken monopoly sign shape without lettering on the dock. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Gibbons read the commerce clause broadly to cover navigation among the states.
img.title: STEAMBOATS AND COMMERCE

questions.question: North Carolina's judicial branch is a unified court system. Its two trial divisions are District Court and Superior Court. Which case belongs in Superior Court?
questions.correctAnswer: A felony murder trial with a jury
distractors: A traffic ticket contested by a driver
A small-claims case over a $3,000 repair bill
A child custody hearing
questions.explanation: Superior Court is NC's general-jurisdiction trial court: felonies, civil claims above $25,000, and jury trials. District Court handles misdemeanors, family law, juvenile cases, and smaller civil claims, usually without juries. Both belong to one unified system topped by the appellate division.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Felonies and juries go up to Superior Court.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a courthouse with two courtroom doors side by side, one grand with tall columns and one modest, a directory board between them kept blank and unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Felony jury trials belong in NC Superior Court.
img.title: TWO TRIAL COURTS

questions.question: North Carolina selects its judges differently from the federal system and from many states: NC judges and justices are chosen by:
questions.correctAnswer: Partisan election - candidates run with party labels; appellate and superior court judges serve eight-year terms, district court judges four-year terms
distractors: Appointment by the governor for life
Merit panels with retention votes only
Election without any party identification allowed
questions.explanation: Since a 2015-2017 series of laws, North Carolina's judicial races - appellate, superior court, and district court - carry party labels again. Appellate and superior court judges serve eight-year terms; district court judges serve four-year terms. Supporters say elections keep judges accountable; critics warn campaigns and party politics can pressure the bench. Judges must retire at age 72 under state law.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: NC judges campaign like politicians - then must judge like judges.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a judge's robe hanging on a stand between a ballot box and a campaign poster board kept entirely blank, symbolic tension, courthouse steps behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC judges run in partisan races - 8-year terms for appellate and superior courts, 4 for district court.
img.title: JUDGES ON THE BALLOT

questions.question: The federal design gives the Senate a unique role in appointments: when the president nominates a Supreme Court justice, the Senate may:
questions.correctAnswer: Confirm or reject the nominee by majority vote after hearings
distractors: Choose a different nominee by two-thirds vote
Require the nominee to win a national referendum
Seat the nominee automatically after 60 days
questions.explanation: Advice and consent is the Senate's great personnel check: hearings, committee votes, and a floor vote. The House plays no role. North Carolina's governor faces no such process for most appointments - but NC voters hold the ultimate check by electing judges themselves.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Senate's half of the appointment power: confirm or reject.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a formal hearing room with a long committee table, microphones, and a single witness chair facing the senators, flags blurred behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Senate confirms or rejects Supreme Court nominees by majority vote.
img.title: CONFIRM OR REJECT

questions.question: North Carolina's constitution gives the General Assembly a check on the governor that Congress does NOT have in the same form: proposing constitutional amendments that:
questions.correctAnswer: Go directly to the voters without the governor's signature or veto
distractors: Require the governor to campaign for them publicly
Take effect immediately upon passage
Must also be approved by the US Congress
questions.explanation: A governor's veto cannot touch a proposed constitutional amendment in North Carolina - three-fifths of each house sends it straight to a referendum. In 2018 voters decided six such amendments at once, a vivid example of the legislature checking executive power through the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Amendments skip the governor's desk entirely - straight to the voters.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a sealed envelope traveling along a path that visibly bypasses a governor's office door and goes directly to a crowd of voters at a ballot box. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC constitutional amendments bypass the governor's veto and go to the voters.
img.title: STRAIGHT TO THE VOTERS

questions.question: The First Amendment protects five freedoms. Which list is complete and correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition
distractors: Religion, speech, press, travel, and privacy
Speech, press, assembly, voting, and arms
Religion, assembly, petition, property, and counsel
questions.explanation: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the government. North Carolina's Declaration of Rights protects the same family of freedoms in Sections 12-14.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Five freedoms in one amendment - religion, speech, press, assembly, petition.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of five symbolic objects on a table - a candle, an open book, a printing press plate, a town-meeting bell, and a rolled petition - under a single beam of light. Petition kept unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The First Amendment protects religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition.
img.title: FIVE FREEDOMS

questions.question: The establishment clause and the free exercise clause of the First Amendment work in tension: together they require government to:
questions.correctAnswer: Neither establish an official religion nor forbid people from practicing their own
distractors: Fund all religions equally from tax revenue
Keep religion out of public view entirely
Let each state choose its official church
questions.explanation: Government must be neutral toward religion: it cannot create a state church (establishment) and cannot suppress worship (free exercise). North Carolina's own constitution once preferred Protestant officeholders in 1776 - a test removed over time, showing how rights protections deepened in both documents.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No state church, no banned faiths - neutrality in both directions.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of several different houses of worship of varied architecture standing along one peaceful street at dusk, none taller or grander than the others, no signs or lettering on any building. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Government may neither establish religion nor prohibit its free exercise.
img.title: NEUTRAL TOWARD FAITH

questions.question: In Engel v. Vitale (1962), the Supreme Court struck down a state-composed school prayer because:
questions.correctAnswer: Government writing and sponsoring prayer for public school students violates the establishment clause
distractors: Students have no right to pray silently on their own
The prayer mentioned a specific denomination by name
Public schools may not employ religious teachers
questions.explanation: New York officials had written a prayer for students to recite daily. The Court held that government may not compose official prayers for schoolchildren - while students' own voluntary prayer remains protected by free exercise. The pair of clauses in one schoolroom.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The state cannot write the prayer; the student may still pray.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a mid-century classroom in the morning with students standing silently, heads in varied postures - some bowed, some looking forward - a teacher at the door, no judgment among them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Engel: government-composed school prayer violates the establishment clause.
img.title: WHO WRITES THE PRAYER

questions.question: Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) held that public school students:
questions.correctAnswer: Do not 'shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate'
distractors: May say anything at school without any limits
Have free speech rights only after age 18
Lose speech rights whenever administrators disagree with them
questions.explanation: Students wore black armbands protesting the Vietnam War. The Court ruled for the students: schools may limit speech only when it substantially disrupts schoolwork or invades others' rights. Tinker is the case every American student should know - it applies in North Carolina classrooms today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rights do not stop at the schoolhouse gate - Tinker said so.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of students walking through a school entrance gate wearing plain black armbands, backpacks and books in hand, a school building behind, calm morning scene. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Tinker: students keep free speech rights at school, short of substantial disruption.
img.title: RIGHTS AT THE GATE

questions.question: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Court protected flag burning as:
questions.correctAnswer: Symbolic speech under the First Amendment - government may not ban expression because society finds it offensive
distractors: A form of petition requiring a permit
Commercial speech subject to full regulation
Conduct wholly outside the First Amendment
questions.explanation: Gregory Johnson burned a flag in protest and was convicted under a Texas flag-desecration law. The Court held 5-4 that the state may not prohibit expression simply because it offends - the flag's protection covers even those who dishonor it. North Carolina's own flag-desecration law fell under the same logic.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The First Amendment protects even speech that shocks - Johnson.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a single flag on a pole at the center of a courthouse square with citizens expressing many views around it at a distance, orderly and dignified, dusk light. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Flag burning is symbolic speech; offensiveness alone cannot justify a ban.
img.title: SPEECH THAT OFFENDS

questions.question: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. Evidence police obtain through an unconstitutional search must generally be excluded from trial. This is the:
questions.correctAnswer: Exclusionary rule, applied to the states in Mapp v. Ohio (1961)
distractors: Good-faith exception, created in United States v. Leon (1984)
Double jeopardy doctrine
Miranda rule, from Miranda v. Arizona
questions.explanation: Dollree Mapp's home was searched without a valid warrant; the Court held that evidence seized in violation of the Fourth Amendment cannot be used in state trials. The rule deters illegal searches by removing their payoff - it governs police work in North Carolina every day.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Illegal search, unusable evidence - that is the exclusionary rule.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a police officer pausing at a closed front door, warrant paperwork absent from his empty hand, while a judge's silhouette reviews a document in an inset courthouse scene. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Mapp v. Ohio applied the exclusionary rule to the states.
img.title: NO WARRANT, NO EVIDENCE

questions.question: The Miranda warnings ('You have the right to remain silent...') come from Miranda v. Arizona (1966), which rests on the Fifth Amendment right against:
questions.correctAnswer: Self-incrimination - compelling a person to testify against themselves
distractors: Unreasonable searches of their home
Cruel and unusual punishment
Double jeopardy in successive trials
questions.explanation: Ernesto Miranda was interrogated for hours without being told he could stay silent or have a lawyer. The Court required warnings before custodial questioning so the privilege against self-incrimination is real, not theoretical - and North Carolina officers give the same warnings for the same reason.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Miranda warnings make the right to silence more than words on paper.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a small card held in a police officer's hand facing a seated suspect in an interview room, the card's print blurred and unreadable, a lawyer's empty chair beside the suspect. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Miranda warnings protect the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.
img.title: THE RIGHT TO REMAIN SILENT

questions.question: Before Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), a poor defendant in a state felony trial could be forced to defend himself without a lawyer. The Court unanimously held that:
questions.correctAnswer: The Sixth Amendment right to counsel is fundamental and states must provide attorneys to defendants who cannot afford them
distractors: Only federal courts must provide counsel
Defendants may have counsel only in capital cases
States could choose whether counsel was necessary case by case
questions.explanation: Clarence Gideon, charged in Florida, represented himself and lost; from prison he petitioned in pencil. The Court held counsel is 'an essential of a fair trial.' North Carolina's public defender system exists because Gideon binds the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No lawyer, no fair trial - Gideon made counsel a right, not a luxury.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a hand-written petition in pencil on lined prison paper beside a law book, the handwriting suggested as faint lines without readable words, light falling across the desk. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Gideon: states must provide counsel to poor felony defendants.
img.title: A LAWYER FOR THE POOR

questions.question: The Bill of Rights originally limited only the federal government (Barron v. Baltimore, 1833). Most of its protections now bind the states through a process called:
questions.correctAnswer: Selective incorporation, using the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause
distractors: Reverse federalism
Judicial federalization by statute
The incorporation doctrine of Article VII
questions.explanation: Beginning in the 20th century, the Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment's promise that no state may deprive a person of liberty without due process 'incorporates' most Bill of Rights protections against state action - case by case, from speech (Gitlow) to counsel (Gideon) to guns (McDonald).
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Fourteenth Amendment carried the Bill of Rights into every statehouse.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a bridge of fourteen arches spanning from a distant federal capitol to a state capitol in the foreground, citizens crossing freely in both directions. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Selective incorporation applies most Bill of Rights protections to the states.
img.title: THE FOURTEENTH BRIDGE

questions.question: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) by declaring that in public education:
questions.correctAnswer: 'Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal' and violate the equal protection clause
distractors: States must spend identical sums on every school
Private schools were abolished nationwide
School boards could no longer set attendance zones
questions.explanation: A unanimous Court held that separating children by race stamps them with a badge of inferiority no facility spending can cure. Brown reached North Carolina directly - the Pearsall Plan and school closings that followed in the state are part of the FPCL-era story of constitutional principles meeting resistance.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Separate is inherently unequal - Brown, unanimous.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of Black and white children walking together up the steps of a brick public school in the 1950s, books in arms, parents watching from the sidewalk, hopeful morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Brown: separate public schools are inherently unequal.
img.title: INHERENTLY UNEQUAL

questions.question: The equal protection clause belongs to which amendment, ratified in 1868 as part of Reconstruction?
questions.correctAnswer: The Fourteenth Amendment - citizenship, due process, and equal protection in one package
distractors: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment
questions.explanation: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) defined citizenship to overturn Dred Scott, barred states from abridging privileges or immunities, required due process, and guaranteed equal protection of the laws. It is the single most litigated amendment in American law - and a mirror of NC's own 'law of the land' clause.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1868's Fourteenth - citizenship, due process, equal protection.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of three tall stone tablets standing together on a courthouse lawn etched with abstract patterns rather than words, citizens of many backgrounds walking past. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Fourteenth Amendment carries equal protection (1868).
img.title: THE RECONSTRUCTION AMENDMENT

questions.question: A museum plaque states: 'The Emancipation Proclamation abolished slavery throughout the United States in 1863.' A historian would correct the plaque because:
questions.correctAnswer: The Proclamation freed enslaved people only in the rebellious states; slavery was abolished everywhere by the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in 1865
distractors: The Proclamation was an act of Congress, not of the president
Slavery was actually abolished by the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870
The Proclamation applied only within the District of Columbia
questions.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment (December 1865) ended slavery and involuntary servitude nationwide except as punishment for crime. Note the distractor trap: the Emancipation Proclamation was a wartime executive order, not an amendment, and freed only those enslaved in rebellious states.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Proclamation freed some; the Thirteenth Amendment freed all - 1865.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of heavy iron chains broken open on a stone floor with light pouring through a doorway behind them, a folded legal document lying beside the chains unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in 1865.
img.title: CHAINS BROKEN BY AMENDMENT

questions.question: The Fifteenth, Nineteenth, Twenty-Fourth, and Twenty-Sixth Amendments share a common theme. Each one:
questions.correctAnswer: Expanded the right to vote - by race, by sex, by ending poll taxes, and by lowering the voting age to 18
distractors: Limited the terms of elected officials
Changed the procedure for amending the Constitution
Shifted taxing power from states to Congress
questions.explanation: Voting amendments tell the story of American democracy widening: race (1870), sex (1920), wealth via poll tax (1964), and age (1971). North Carolina's own history includes the shameful counterpoint - the 1900 suffrage amendment whose literacy test and poll tax disfranchised Black voters for decades.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four amendments, one direction - a wider electorate.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a doorway widening across four panels of time, with voters of different eras and backgrounds passing through more easily in each successive panel. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The 15th, 19th, 24th, and 26th Amendments each expanded voting rights.
img.title: WIDENING THE DOOR

questions.question: Amending the US Constitution under Article V requires, in the usual route:
questions.correctAnswer: Proposal by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states
distractors: Proposal by the president and approval by a national majority vote
Ratification by a simple majority of state governors
Proposal by nine states and approval by the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Only 27 amendments have survived this demanding double supermajority in more than 230 years - by design. Compare North Carolina: three-fifths of each legislative house proposes, and a simple majority of voters ratifies - state constitutions are meant to be more changeable than the federal one.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds to propose, three-fourths to ratify - hard on purpose.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a very heavy stone door with two large keys held by different groups of people on either side, both keys needed to open it, symbolizing double supermajorities. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Article V: two-thirds propose, three-fourths ratify.
img.title: A DELIBERATELY HARD DOOR

questions.question: New Jersey v. T.L.O. (1985), a case about a school search, produced a rule every NC student lives under: school officials may search a student when:
questions.correctAnswer: They have reasonable suspicion the search will reveal evidence of a rule or law violation - a lower standard than police probable cause
distractors: They obtain a search warrant from a judge first
The student has been arrested for a felony
Any teacher requests it for any reason
questions.explanation: Balancing students' Fourth Amendment rights against schools' need for order, the Court allowed searches justified at their inception and reasonable in scope. Your backpack in a North Carolina hallway is governed by T.L.O.'s 'reasonableness' standard, not the warrant rule that protects your home.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: At school the standard is reasonable suspicion, not a warrant - T.L.O.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a school principal and a student standing beside an open locker in a quiet hallway, a vice principal holding a purse found inside, respectful and procedural mood. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T.L.O.: school searches need reasonable suspicion, not a warrant.
img.title: SEARCHED AT SCHOOL

questions.question: Citizens United v. FEC (2010) remains controversial because the Court held that limiting independent political spending by corporations and unions violates:
questions.correctAnswer: The First Amendment - political spending is a form of speech the government may not restrict by speaker identity
distractors: The right of corporations to vote in elections
The commerce clause's grant of regulatory power
States' rights to run their own elections
questions.explanation: The 5-4 decision struck down limits on independent expenditures, reasoning that the First Amendment does not allow silencing speakers because they are corporations. Critics argue it unleashed money's influence; defenders call it core political speech. FPCL students weigh it as a live founding-principles debate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Money as speech - Citizens United split the Court and the country.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a television studio camera pointed at a giant screen of campaign advertisements kept abstract and unreadable, stacks of printed flyers blurred in the foreground. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Citizens United treated independent political spending as protected speech.
img.title: MONEY AND SPEECH

questions.question: North Carolina's Declaration of Rights protects the right to keep and bear arms in Section 30 - but unlike the federal Second Amendment debate, NC courts have long held the state right is:
questions.correctAnswer: Subject to reasonable regulation by the General Assembly for public safety
distractors: Absolute and beyond any legislative control
Limited to members of the National Guard only
Identical in scope to hunting licenses
questions.explanation: Section 30 ties the right to the militia tradition, and NC courts have consistently held it is subject to reasonable, non-prohibitive regulation tied to public peace and safety (State v. Dawson) - for example, the text itself allows penal laws against carrying concealed weapons. The regulation must still be reasonable: in Britt v. State (2009) the NC Supreme Court held a blanket felon firearms ban unconstitutional as applied to a nonviolent offender.
