It is a case study in how state declarations of rights grow their own case law independent of federal doctrine.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: NC's arms right is real - and reasonably regulable, say its courts.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a colonial-era flintlock musket resting in a museum case beside a modern hunting rifle tag kept blank, courthouse visible through the museum window. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC's Section 30 arms right is subject to reasonable regulation.
img.title: A RIGHT WITH RULES

questions.question: The right to a trial by jury appears in BOTH the US Constitution's orbit and Section 24-25 tradition of state declarations. In North Carolina criminal trials, a peculiar rule survives: a jury's verdict must be:
questions.correctAnswer: Unanimous - all twelve jurors must agree to convict
distractors: By a three-fourths majority of jurors
By simple majority vote of the jury
Decided by the judge if jurors split evenly
questions.explanation: North Carolina has kept the common-law unanimity rule for criminal verdicts throughout its history, and the US Supreme Court's Ramos v. Louisiana (2020) extended the same requirement to all states. Unanimity is the jury system's strongest protection against rushed convictions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twelve jurors, one voice - conviction in NC must be unanimous.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of twelve jurors seated in two rows in a jury box, all turning to face the judge together in unison, wood-paneled courtroom. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC criminal verdicts must be unanimous - all twelve jurors.
img.title: TWELVE, SPEAKING AS ONE

questions.question: In 1776, North Carolina's Declaration of Rights condemned taxation without representation. Its Section on elections also insisted representatives should be chosen in:
questions.correctAnswer: Frequent, free elections - so that representatives remain accountable to the people
distractors: Elections held once every ten years
Lotteries among property owners
Hereditary succession within districts
questions.explanation: The 1776 declaration paired grievances with machinery: frequent elections keep representatives dependent on the people's will. That is why NC legislators still face voters every two years - the shortest accountability loop in the system, straight from the founding document.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Frequent elections keep representatives on a short leash - a 1776 idea still at work.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an election calendar wheel turning in a cycle beside a ballot box, seasons changing around it in the background, abstract and symbolic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The NC Declaration of Rights demands frequent, free elections.
img.title: FREQUENT ELECTIONS

questions.question: Freedom of the press protects newspapers and broadcasters, but the Supreme Court has allowed prior restraint (government censorship before publication) almost never. The leading case is:
questions.correctAnswer: Near v. Minnesota (1931), which struck down a state law shutting down 'malicious' newspapers
distractors: Schenck v. United States (1919), which approved all wartime censorship
Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988), which banned all student newspapers
Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), which licensed sedition trials
questions.explanation: Near made prior restraint presumptively unconstitutional and incorporated press freedom against the states. Later, the Pentagon Papers case (1971) applied the same heavy presumption when the government tried to stop publication of a classified history - the press usually wins before, and answers after, publication.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Government almost never gets to censor first - Near v. Minnesota.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a vintage printing press rolling out newspapers while a large pair of scissors hangs locked in a glass case on the wall, symbolic of censorship restrained. Newspapers shown with abstract lines, not readable text. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Near v. Minnesota: prior restraint of the press is presumptively unconstitutional.
img.title: NO CENSOR'S SCISSORS

questions.question: The Eighth Amendment's ban on 'cruel and unusual punishments' has been interpreted by the courts through:
questions.correctAnswer: The 'evolving standards of decency' of society - punishments once accepted may become unconstitutional
distractors: The exact punishments listed as cruel in 1791, frozen forever
A national referendum held every generation
Each state's unlimited discretion to define cruelty
questions.explanation: From Trop v. Dulles (1958) onward, the Court measures punishments against contemporary standards - striking down, for example, execution of juveniles (Roper v. Simmons, 2005) and of people with intellectual disabilities (Atkins v. Virginia, 2002). Doctrine evolves; the text does not.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The words stay; the standards evolve - that is the Eighth Amendment's story.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a stone inscription wall photographed in two eras side by side - aged and dark on the left, freshly lit on the right - with the same abstract carved lines, symbolizing old text and new light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Eighth Amendment meaning follows evolving standards of decency.
img.title: OLD WORDS, NEW STANDARDS

questions.question: North Carolina's constitution contains a right NOT expressly found in the US Constitution: Article IX, Section 2(1) guarantees a general and uniform system of free public schools, and Section 9 adds that the benefits of the state's public institutions of higher education shall, as far as practicable, be extended to the people of the State free of expense. This shows state constitutions can:
questions.correctAnswer: Guarantee positive rights and services beyond the federal floor of protections
distractors: Only repeat the federal Bill of Rights word for word
Never mention education at all
Override the US Constitution when they conflict
questions.explanation: Federal constitutional law mostly limits government; state constitutions also command it to act - to fund schools, in NC's case. The Leandro litigation grew from these state words alone, proving state constitutions are living sources of rights, not echoes of the federal text.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The US Constitution mostly says 'don't'; NC's also says 'provide schools.'

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of children entering a bright public school through doors held wide open, a cornerstone with an abstract carved pattern, morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: State constitutions can add positive rights like free public education.
img.title: RIGHTS BEYOND THE FLOOR

questions.question: A Miranda warning is NOT required when:
questions.correctAnswer: A person volunteers statements without being in custody and interrogated - the warnings attach to custodial interrogation
distractors: Police question a suspect at the station for any reason
The suspect is under the age of 30
The crime under investigation is a misdemeanor
questions.explanation: Miranda protects against compelled self-incrimination during custodial interrogation. A suspect who is free to leave, or who blurts out a statement unasked, stands outside the rule - though the statement's voluntariness can still be challenged. Knowing where a right's boundary lies is as civic as knowing the right itself.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Miranda guards the interrogation room - not every conversation with police.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a bright open street scene with a citizen chatting freely with an officer on a sidewalk, contrasted with a closed interview room door in shadow at the edge of the frame. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Miranda warnings attach only to custodial interrogation.
img.title: WHERE RIGHTS BEGIN AND END

questions.question: The Second Amendment, as interpreted in District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), protects:
questions.correctAnswer: An individual's right to possess a handgun in the home for self-defense
distractors: A state's right to disarm all private citizens
Only the right of militias to store weapons in armories
An unlimited right to carry any weapon anywhere
questions.explanation: Heller held the amendment protects an individual right centered on self-defense in the home, while noting longstanding regulations (felon bans, sensitive-place rules) remain permissible. Bruen (2022) later reframed the test around text, history, and tradition.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Heller: an individual right at home - with room for longstanding rules.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a modest home doorway with a secure lockbox on a shelf inside, a family home at dusk, emphasis on safety and the home rather than weaponry detail. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Heller protects an individual right to a handgun at home for self-defense.
img.title: THE RIGHT AT HOME

questions.question: Students often ask: if North Carolina has its own Declaration of Rights, why does the federal Bill of Rights still matter here? The best answer is:
questions.correctAnswer: The two documents set overlapping floors - whichever protects the citizen more in a given case controls, and both bind NC officials
distractors: The state declaration replaced the federal one in 1971
Federal rights apply only inside Washington, D.C.
The NC document is symbolic and has no legal force
questions.explanation: Federal rights bind every state through the Fourteenth Amendment; state rights bind state officials directly and can protect MORE than the federal floor, never less. A North Carolinian in court can invoke both - lawyers call it raising claims under both constitutions.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two floors of rights - you stand on whichever is higher.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a staircase with two broad landings, a citizen standing on the higher landing looking out over a valley of courthouses, symbolic of overlapping protections. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Both constitutions bind NC officials; the more protective right controls.
img.title: TWO FLOORS OF FREEDOM

questions.question: Under the Fourteenth Amendment, a person becomes a United States citizen by:
questions.correctAnswer: Being born on US soil or naturalized under federal law - citizenship by birth is called jus soli
distractors: Registering with the state within 30 days of birth
Declaring loyalty before a county clerk at age 18
Being born only to two citizen parents
questions.explanation: The amendment's first sentence reversed Dred Scott: 'All persons born or naturalized in the United States... are citizens.' Birthright citizenship (jus soli, law of the soil) makes nearly every child born in North Carolina a citizen of the United States and of North Carolina at once.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Born here, citizen here - jus soli, the law of the soil.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a newborn's footprint pressed in ink beside a folded flag in a maternity ward window light, symbolic and tender, no faces shown close. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: US citizenship comes by birth on US soil or by naturalization.
img.title: CITIZEN BY BIRTH

questions.question: Naturalization is the process by which an immigrant becomes a US citizen. Which requirement is part of that federal process?
questions.correctAnswer: Passing tests in English and in US civics and history, and swearing an oath of allegiance
distractors: Serving two years in the state militia
Winning election to a local office first
Owning property in the United States for five years
questions.explanation: Federal law requires lawful permanent residence, good moral character, an interview, English and civics examinations, and the oath. North Carolina hosts naturalization ceremonies in its federal courthouses - new citizens who immediately gain the vote the FPCL course studies.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: English, civics, and an oath - the naturalization path.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a naturalization ceremony in a courthouse, new citizens of many origins raising their right hands together, small flags in their other hands, joyful solemnity. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Naturalization requires English and civics tests and an oath of allegiance.
img.title: THE OATH

questions.question: A civic DUTY differs from a civic RESPONSIBILITY in that a duty is:
questions.correctAnswer: Required by law - like paying taxes, obeying laws, and serving on a jury when summoned
distractors: Something only elected officials must do
Optional but praiseworthy, like volunteering
Enforced by public opinion rather than courts
questions.explanation: Duties carry legal consequences: tax evasion is a crime, ignoring a jury summons can bring contempt. Responsibilities - voting, staying informed, volunteering - are the voluntary habits a republic needs but cannot compel. Founding Principles courses hammer this distinction every year.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Duties are the law's demands; responsibilities are citizenship's habits.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two columns of symbolic objects: legal scales and a tax form kept blank on the left, a ballot and a volunteer's helping hands on the right, balanced presentation. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Duties are legally required; responsibilities are voluntary but vital.
img.title: DUTY VS. RESPONSIBILITY

questions.question: Jury service is sometimes called 'the citizen's share of the judicial power.' In North Carolina, jurors for Superior Court trials are drawn from:
questions.correctAnswer: Lists of registered voters and licensed drivers in the county - ordinary citizens deciding facts
distractors: A standing panel of retired judges
Volunteers who apply at the courthouse each year
Students enrolled in civics courses
questions.explanation: County master jury lists combine voter registration and DMV records so the pool mirrors the community. The jury is federalism's and democracy's meeting point: neighbors, not officials, decide guilt in serious cases - and in NC their verdict must be unanimous.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Jurors are the people inside the judicial branch.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of citizens of many ages and backgrounds receiving summons envelopes and walking into a county courthouse in the morning, ordinary clothes, civic mood. Envelopes kept blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC jurors are drawn from voter and driver lists in the county.
img.title: THE PEOPLE JUDGE

questions.question: North Carolina holds its state elections in even-numbered years, and ALL 170 General Assembly seats are on the ballot each time because:
questions.correctAnswer: Every member of both houses serves a two-year term
distractors: Federal law requires state elections every two years
The governor orders a full election each cycle
North Carolina has no staggered terms for any office
questions.explanation: Two-year terms for both chambers mean the entire legislature can be replaced in a single election - the most direct accountability in NC government. Contrast the US Senate's staggered six-year terms, designed for insulation rather than responsiveness.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The whole Assembly faces the voters every two years - maximum accountability.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a giant ballot box on a plaza with lines of voters stretching around a legislative building at sunrise, festive democratic mood. Ballots kept blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: All 170 Assembly seats are elected every two years.
img.title: EVERY SEAT, EVERY CYCLE

questions.question: Early voting ('one-stop' voting) in North Carolina lets a registered voter:
questions.correctAnswer: Cast a ballot in person at designated sites in the weeks before Election Day, and register-and-vote the same day during that period
distractors: Vote by text message from home
Vote in any state where they happen to be traveling
Cast two ballots if they also vote on Election Day
questions.explanation: One-stop sites open across each county during the early-voting period, and eligible citizens may register and vote in the same visit there. On Election Day itself, voters must appear at their assigned precinct. These mechanics decide real turnout - and are set by the State Board of Elections and county boards.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One-stop = register and vote in one trip, before Election Day.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of voters checking in at tables inside a community recreation center weeks before an election, poll workers with laptops, a line of citizens of all ages. Screens and papers kept abstract. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC one-stop early voting allows voting before Election Day at county sites.
img.title: ONE-STOP VOTING

questions.question: North Carolina's State Board of Elections and the 100 county boards administer elections. This structure is an example of:
questions.correctAnswer: Administered federalism - a state system run locally, where national rules set floors but counties run the actual voting
distractors: Complete federal control of elections
Private administration by political parties
Judicial management of all election disputes
questions.explanation: The Elections Clause lets states run even federal elections, subject to Congress's rules. In NC that means state standards, county execution: polling places, ballots, and counts are local work, one reason election rules differ across state lines within one nation.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Washington sets the floor; your county runs the polling place.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a wall-sized map of a state with one hundred county shapes each marked by a small pin, connected by threads to a central board table, map abstract without labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC elections are administered by a state board and 100 county boards.
img.title: STATE STANDARDS, COUNTY WORK

questions.question: Political parties serve American democracy mainly by:
questions.correctAnswer: Organizing voters, recruiting candidates, and offering competing platforms that simplify choices
distractors: Counting the official ballots on election night
Writing the platforms required by the Constitution
Appointing judges to federal courts
questions.explanation: Parties are not in the Constitution - Madison feared them as factions - yet they became the machinery of mass democracy: they recruit, fund, brand, and mobilize. North Carolina's primaries nominate the candidates whom November's general election decides between.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties are unofficial but indispensable machinery of democracy.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of two large tents at a county fair with crowds of citizens moving between information tables, banners kept as blank colored shapes, festive civic atmosphere. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Parties recruit candidates, organize voters, and offer competing platforms.
img.title: DEMOCRACY'S MACHINERY

questions.question: A primary election differs from a general election because a primary:
questions.correctAnswer: Selects each party's nominees who will face the voters in the general election
distractors: Is held only in presidential years
Determines which laws take effect immediately
Chooses electors for the Electoral College directly
questions.explanation: Think of it as a two-round system: primaries narrow the field inside each party (in NC, a candidate needs 30 percent to avoid a runoff under current law), and the general election chooses the officeholder. Low primary turnout gives small, motivated electorates outsized power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Primaries pick the nominees; the general election picks the winner.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a tournament-bracket style garden path with many gates narrowing to two final doors and then one open gateway, citizens walking the path, symbolic and clear. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Primaries choose party nominees; general elections choose officeholders.
img.title: TWO ROUNDS

questions.question: North Carolina is one of the states where unaffiliated voters may participate in primaries. Under NC law, an unaffiliated voter at a primary may:
questions.correctAnswer: Choose one party's primary ballot to vote in that election (or an unaffiliated ballot if available)
distractors: Vote in every party's primary on the same day
Vote only if a party chair invites them
Skip the primary but cast two general-election ballots
questions.explanation: Unaffiliated voters are now the largest registration group in North Carolina. The one-ballot choice keeps primaries party-run while letting independents influence nominations - a live design question about who should choose a party's standard-bearer.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Unaffiliated in NC? Pick ONE party's primary ballot.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a voter at a check-in table being offered two differently colored blank ballot folders and selecting one, poll worker nodding, other voters behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC unaffiliated voters choose one party's primary ballot.
img.title: PICK ONE BALLOT

questions.question: During a legislative session, the North Carolina Chamber of Commerce publishes research, meets with legislators, and runs ads supporting a tax bill - yet its name never appears on any ballot. Which feature makes the Chamber an interest group rather than a political party?
questions.correctAnswer: It tries to influence policy without nominating or running its own candidates for office
distractors: It is forbidden by law to discuss elections in public
It is registered as an agency of the state government
It operates only at the national level, never in Raleigh
questions.explanation: Groups like the NC Chamber, teachers' associations, and environmental councils lobby, publish research, endorse, and fund independent ads - but the name on the ballot is never theirs. Madison's answer to factions applies: many groups checking one another in an extended republic.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Parties run candidates; interest groups run arguments.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of representatives of many occupations - farmers, teachers, nurses, builders - carrying different shaped signs kept blank into a hearing room, orderly and civic. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Interest groups influence policy without running candidates.
img.title: ARGUMENTS, NOT CANDIDATES

questions.question: Lobbying the General Assembly is protected activity in America because the First Amendment guarantees the right to:
questions.correctAnswer: Petition the government for a redress of grievances
distractors: A government job in exchange for support
Anonymous bribery of public officials
Speak without any disclosure requirements whatsoever
questions.explanation: Petition is the often-forgotten fifth freedom of the First Amendment. North Carolina regulates lobbying with registration and reporting - transparency rules the courts allow - but the act of asking your government for change is itself a founding right, exercised in Raleigh daily.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lobbying's root is a First Amendment right - to petition.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a citizen handing a folder of documents to a legislator in the corridor of a legislative building, both standing in open daylight, folder cover kept blank. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Lobbying rests on the First Amendment right to petition.
img.title: THE FIFTH FREEDOM

questions.question: During a hurricane emergency, North Carolina's governor issues evacuation orders and deploys the National Guard. These actions rest on the governor's role as:
questions.correctAnswer: Chief executive of the state and commander-in-chief of its military forces (unless federalized)
distractors: A member of the federal cabinet
Commander of the state Supreme Court
An officer of the Federal Emergency Management Agency
questions.explanation: The NC Emergency Management Act channels broad powers through the governor: declaring emergencies, ordering evacuations of the Outer Banks, and activating the Guard. Federal help (FEMA) arrives on request, but the constitutional first responder is the state - federalism in a storm.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In a hurricane, the governor is NC's first responder-in-chief.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of rescue trucks and National Guard vehicles moving through a flooded coastal street at dusk, sandbags and a command tent, citizens being helped into boats, organized urgency. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The governor commands NC's emergency response and National Guard.
img.title: FIRST RESPONDER-IN-CHIEF

questions.question: Counties in North Carolina derive their powers from the state, not from their own inherent sovereignty. Lawyers summarize this with Dillon's Rule:
questions.correctAnswer: Local governments possess only powers granted by the state, expressly or by fair implication
distractors: Counties may do anything the state has not forbidden
Cities are sovereign nations within their borders
County power comes from the US Constitution directly
questions.explanation: Named for Judge John Dillon, the rule makes municipalities and counties creatures of the state: the General Assembly creates counties, empowers city councils, and may restructure them. North Carolina softens the rule with statutes directing broad construction of local powers - but the hierarchy stands: state first, local by grant.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Local power is borrowed power - Dillon's Rule.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a chain of authority drawn as light flowing downward through three levels of platforms - state capitol, county courthouse, town hall - each platform smaller than the one above. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Dillon's Rule: local governments hold only state-granted powers.
img.title: BORROWED POWER

questions.question: A North Carolina city council votes on zoning rules for a new neighborhood, the county school board sets school policies, and the General Assembly passes a state budget. The single principle that explains why different bodies decide different questions is:
questions.correctAnswer: Federalism and separation of powers operating together - authority is divided by level and by function
distractors: The spoils system of appointing loyal supporters
Direct democracy in all public decisions
Judicial supremacy over all policy questions
questions.explanation: Two grids cross: vertically, federalism assigns questions to nation, state, or locality; horizontally, separation of powers assigns lawmaking, executing, and judging within each level. FPCL's final analysis standard (CL.C&G.2/4) asks students to locate any real decision on that grid - as this question does.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Every decision sits somewhere on the grid - level across, function down.

questions.question: Local media and statewide newspapers matter to the founding design because the founders counted on an informed citizenry. The modern challenge most often cited is:
questions.correctAnswer: The collapse of local news coverage leaves many NC communities as 'news deserts' with little watchdog reporting
distractors: Newspapers are banned from covering state government
Citizens are legally forbidden to discuss politics online
The state operates all television stations in North Carolina
questions.explanation: Hundreds of NC local papers have closed or shrunk since 2005, even as national partisan media boomed. Research ties vanished local coverage to lower turnout and less competitive local elections - a founding-principles problem wearing modern clothes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No local watchdog, quieter democracy - the news desert problem.

Newspaper kept unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Falling local news coverage weakens the informed citizenry the founders assumed.
img.title: NEWS DESERTS

questions.question: A student reads a claim online that North Carolina has abolished early voting. Before sharing it, the founding-principles habit of 'recurrence to fundamental principles' suggests first:
questions.correctAnswer: Checking the claim against primary and reliable sources - the actual statute and the State Board of Elections
distractors: Sharing it quickly so others can judge
Assuming it is true because it appeared many times
Asking whether it supports the student's preferred party
questions.explanation: FPCL standards teach evaluation of sources as a civic skill: go to the law itself and the administering agency before amplifying a claim. In this case the statute books and the NCSBE show early voting alive and scheduled - the claim is false, and the check took minutes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Check the statute before you share the claim.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a student at a library table comparing a phone screen kept abstract against a thick statute book and an official pamphlet kept blurred, magnifying glass in hand. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Verify civic claims against the statute and the administering agency.
img.title: CHECK THE SOURCE

questions.question: The North Carolina Constitution's Article IX was the legal foundation when the state Supreme Court decided Leandro. The article commands the General Assembly to provide:
questions.correctAnswer: 'A general and uniform system of free public schools' for all children of the state
distractors: Equal funding for every private academy
A university in every county seat
Free textbooks for college students only
questions.explanation: The 1868 constitution wrote this command, and the 1971 constitution kept it. Leandro read those words as guaranteeing each child an opportunity for a sound basic education - an example of a state constitution doing work the federal one does not, since the US Constitution never mentions education.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article IX promises the school system; Leandro enforced the promise.

img.tip: Article IX commands a general and uniform system of free public schools.
img.title: THE SCHOOL PROMISE

questions.question: In 2018 North Carolina voters approved an amendment capping the state income tax rate in the constitution itself. Whatever one's view of the policy, the episode demonstrates:
questions.correctAnswer: The amendment power in action - the General Assembly proposed by three-fifths and the people ratified directly
distractors: The governor signing a tax bill into law
The state Supreme Court setting tax policy
Congress amending a state constitution for the first time
questions.explanation: The tax-cap amendment (capping the rate at 7 percent) traveled the full Article XIII road: proposal by supermajority of the legislature, no gubernatorial veto possible, majority approval by voters. It shows amendments as a tool majorities can use to bind future legislatures.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Amendments can lock in policy - three-fifths propose, the people decide.

img.tip: The 2018 tax cap shows NC's amendment process binding future legislatures.
img.title: LOCKING IT IN

questions.question: North Carolina's Supreme Court in Harper v. Hall wrestled with partisan gerrymandering of the state's own maps - first striking maps down, then, after the court's membership changed, rehearing and reversing. The episode's deepest civics lesson is that:
questions.correctAnswer: Constitutional meaning in a state can shift with the elected judiciary - a consequence of choosing judges by election
distractors: State courts may never review election maps
Gerrymandering questions belong to Congress alone
Courts always agree on constitutional interpretation
questions.explanation: Because NC elects its justices, a change in the court's majority changed the law of redistricting within a single election cycle - first (2022) reading the state constitution to forbid partisan gerrymandering, then (2023) withdrawing that reading. FPCL treats it as the state's leading modern case study in judicial power and its discontents.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Elected judges mean constitutional law can turn with an election - Harper v. Hall.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a balance scale with district map shapes piled on one pan slowly tipping, then being rebalanced by a robed hand, courthouse pillars behind, abstract maps without labels. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Harper v. Hall shows elected courts can reverse constitutional readings as membership changes.
img.title: WHEN COURTS CHANGE COURSE

questions.question: The initiative and referendum are tools of direct democracy used in about half the states. In North Carolina:
questions.correctAnswer: There is NO statewide citizen initiative - only the General Assembly can propose amendments and laws, though voters ratify amendments
distractors: Citizens may place any law on the ballot with 5,000 signatures
The governor may call referendums at will on any topic
Counties may nullify state laws by referendum
questions.explanation: North Carolina is a representative-democracy state at the state level: no initiative, no popular referendum on statutes, no recall of state officials. The people's direct constitutional role is ratifying amendments the legislature proposes - a deliberate 1776 choice the state has kept through every constitution since.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No initiative in NC - the people's direct vote is reserved for amendments.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a long petition scroll kept blank being turned away at a capitol door while a formal amendment envelope is carried past toward a ballot box, symbolic contrast. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC has no citizen initiative; voters ratify amendments the Assembly proposes.
img.title: REPRESENTATIVES PROPOSE

questions.question: Recall elections, used in some states to remove officials mid-term, do NOT exist for North Carolina state officials. An NC governor or legislator who loses public trust can be removed early only by:
questions.correctAnswer: Impeachment by the House and trial by the Senate (for impeachable officers), or by the voters at the next regular election
distractors: A petition of 10 percent of voters triggering a recall vote
Order of the state Supreme Court
A vote of the Council of State
questions.explanation: North Carolina kept the founding-era toolkit: fixed terms, frequent elections, and impeachment for serious misconduct. The two-year House and Senate terms mean accountability is never more than one election away - the framers' chosen substitute for recall.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No recall in NC - short terms and impeachment do the job.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a calendar with pages turning rapidly toward an election day sunrise while a formal gavel rests unused in a glass case, symbolic of patience built into the design. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: NC has no recall; removal runs through impeachment or the next election.
img.title: NO RECALL HERE

questions.question: Which scenario best shows the NC and US constitutions working as the FPCL course intends students to see them - as a matched set?
questions.correctAnswer: A Raleigh teenager studies both texts to challenge a school rule: the First Amendment protects her speech, and the NC Declaration of Rights protects it too
distractors: A mayor asks the governor to veto a federal law
A county sheriff enforces a treaty with France
A state senator casts North Carolina's vote in the Electoral College
questions.explanation: The course's very name pairs the two foundings: principles of the United States AND of North Carolina. Citizens live under both documents daily, and skilled citizens argue from whichever text - federal or state - speaks to the question.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two constitutions, one citizen - argue from both.

img.tip: Citizens can invoke both the US and NC constitutions - a matched set.
img.title: A MATCHED SET

questions.question: The framers of North Carolina's first constitution in 1776 and of the US Constitution in 1787 worked in the shadow of the same fear. Their shared design choices - written constitutions, separated powers, declared rights - were all aimed at preventing:
questions.correctAnswer: The concentration of power that had made royal government tyrannical
distractors: The formation of political parties
Trade between the states
The growth of large cities
questions.explanation: Both generations had resisted a king and his governors. Their answer was structural: divide power, write the limits down, declare the rights, and let ambition check ambition. Every topic in the FPCL course is a variation on that single founding decision.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One fear - concentrated power; one answer - divide it and write it down.

Crowns and pages symbolic, writing unreadable. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Written constitutions and separated powers aimed to prevent tyranny.
img.title: THE SHARED FEAR

questions.question: A closing question for the Founding Principles course: a North Carolina citizen who believes a new state law violates her rights has the strongest claim when she can show the law conflicts with:
questions.correctAnswer: Either the US Constitution (through the Fourteenth Amendment) or the North Carolina Constitution - she may plead both, and courts will apply the more protective text
distractors: The Declaration of Independence standing alone
The platform of the majority political party
A resolution passed by her county commissioners
questions.explanation: Declarations inspire and platforms persuade, but courts enforce constitutions. The dual-constitutionalism of the FPCL course ends where citizenship begins: know both texts, plead both texts, and let judges test the law against the higher law of each.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Plead both constitutions - that is the course, and the craft of citizenship.
